metadata.title: Conversation-based assessment: A novel approach to boosting test-taking effort in digital formative assessment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a conceptual discussion of conversation-based assessment (CBA) as a way to address low-stakes non-effortful test-taking in formative assessment, and it does not analyze an ILSA/PISA micro-dataset. Because no student-level assessment dataset, sampling frame, or administered assessment instrument is modeled empirically, there are no survey weights to apply (e.g., no TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT-type variables) and no replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/JRR) is described. If future empirical work uses PISA or other ILSA micro-data to test the proposed mechanism, analysts should apply the complex survey design weights provided by the data source and use the corresponding replicate weights for variance estimation. For the present manuscript, weighting and PV/scaling procedures are not applicable because no scaling or PV-based achievement outcomes are estimated.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The manuscript does not perform an empirical analysis of cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA (e.g., PISA) and therefore does not generate or use Plausible Values (PVs). Instead, it provides a narrative argument and literature-based discussion about how conversational agents could increase test-taking effort in formative and potentially large-scale low-stakes assessments. As a result, missing-data handling for PV-based outcomes is not part of the study’s methodology.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No ILSA/National large-scale assessment micro-data are analyzed. The paper discusses conversation-based assessment (CBA) conceptually and references prior studies (e.g., CBA examples and related work) without defining an analytic sample, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or grade/domain subsample from PISA or any other large-scale assessment.

Instead, it synthesizes prior literature on conversational agents, assessment formats (selected- and constructed-response), and the role of motivation/test-taking effort in validity threats. Because no dataset, countries, or ML pipeline are evaluated, there are no benchmarks to compare and no methodological details on PV handling, missing-data treatment, or survey-weight application. data.null_fields_interpretation: The extraction is sparse because the manuscript does not conduct an original empirical analysis with ILSA micro-data, ML model training, or PV-based achievement estimation. Consequently, fields that normally require dataset/cycle/grade/domain, country-level sample sizes, PV handling, missing-data handling, and ML performance metrics are not populated. The paper’s contribution is theoretical/methodological (a proposed perspective and rationale), so main_findings and confounder/predictor extraction for an ML pipeline are not applicable.
